claims.text: The initial quinary alloy is equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Standardized thermomechanical processing can produce single-phase FCC microstructures in the selected quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Increasing the number of constituent elements broadens the local stacking-fault-energy distribution.
Heterogeneous lattice distortions are responsible for the broader local stacking-fault-energy distribution.
Local stacking-fault-energy heterogeneity modulates competition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
The balance between slip and twinning governs differences in strain hardening and failure behavior among these alloys.
The quinary alloy has a broader stacking-fault-energy distribution than its quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
The broader stacking-fault-energy distribution in the quinary alloy promotes a mixed deformation mechanism involving both dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Quaternary and ternary alloys have narrower stacking-fault-energy ranges than the quinary alloy.
Narrower stacking-fault-energy ranges in the lower-order alloys lead predominantly to dislocation slip or less effective twinning.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary FCC alloys will exhibit lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary FCC alloys will exhibit lower twin-nucleation frequencies.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary FCC alloys will exhibit altered failure modes because of their less diverse stacking-fault-energy profiles.
The quinary alloy will exhibit a balanced combination of slip and twinning.
The quinary alloy has a superior cost-performance trade-off despite higher constituent costs.
Identical processing and testing conditions are proposed for all compositions.
The proposed deformation tests use micropillar compression at approximately 10^-3 s^-1 and at approximately 298 K and 600 K.
High-resolution TEM, EBSD, synchrotron XRD, atom-probe tomography, and chemical mapping can verify local lattice distortions and establish local stacking-fault-energy distributions.
The proposed explanation is limited to single-phase FCC alloys tested under the specified processing, strain-rate, and temperature conditions.
The processing route minimizes solid-solution strengthening, or its contribution can be separately quantified.
